1:
Who the barren woman is decides the chapter. Adam Clarke lists the options—some suppose it addressed to the Gentiles, some to the Jewish church, some to the Christian church in its first stage—and, comparing the parts and especially the seventh and eighth verses, takes its most obvious import to be the future conversion of the Jews and the prosperity of that nation once reconciled. The barren woman he describes as the church confined within the bounds of one nation, and more narrowly still by the small number of true believers; the converted Gentiles he treats as a new accession of adopted children admitted into the original church. John Wesley reads the song as following from what precedes: the prophet, having discoursed of the sufferings of Christ, and foreseeing the glorious state of the church, breaks out into this triumph, so that as the foregoing chapter speaks literally of Christ, this speaks of the church of Christ, barren until his coming. Charles Ellicott makes the connection formally: the words carry on the jubilant strain of the chapters before, leaving the passage about the suffering servant as a mysterious episode inserted, it may be, to show how the restoration had become possible; and takes the children of the desolate for the returning exiles primarily and ultimately for all citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem.

Matthew Henry works both levels. Applied to the return from captivity, it promises that a city which had been like a wife written childless should be replenished and the country peopled again, the suburbs extended, and estates long wrongfully held returned to their right owners. He supports it with numbers: those who first came out of Babylon were but forty-two thousand, a fifteenth of the multitude that had come out of Egypt, yet five centuries later a reckoning from the number of the paschal lambs put the nation at nearly three millions. But the promise must be applied, he says, to the church of God in general, and describes the state it was in before: the church lay in a little compass and brought forth little fruit, few proselytes were added, serious godliness lost ground, and the children of God were scattered like those of a broken and reduced family, making no figure in the world.

The enlarging of the tent is read closely. Keil and Delitzsch observe that she is to widen the space within her tent while others spread out its coverings, the verb having no definite subject, as often where some subordinate servant is meant; and they catch the point of the prohibition—she is not to forbid the work, saying in her weakness of faith that the tent is good enough as it is and would be too large. The cords she is to lengthen and the pegs to ram fast into the earth, because the dwelling has now much more to receive. John Gill explains why a tent is the figure: the church is compared to one because of its uncertain and movable condition, and because of its outward meanness and small extent—whereas now room is to be made for an accession of inhabitants, the gospel church state not being confined to Jerusalem. Wesley puts it plainly: enlarged to be capable of the Gentiles, strengthened that the stakes may bear the greater weight. On the breaking forth Ellicott notes that right and left strictly mean north and south to one looking eastward, and here mean simply on every side, the words following having a lower material and a higher spiritual meaning together. Keil and Delitzsch add that east and west must be supplied too, since the ancient promises of extent remained unfulfilled even in the age of David and Solomon. Gill piles up comparisons—an inundation that breaks its banks, a warehouse so overstocked that the walls burst, or a country grown so populous that the inhabitants pass their borders to seek new settlements.
4:
The two reproaches named are identified the same way by everyone. Adam Clarke and Charles Ellicott both take the shame of youth for the Egyptian bondage and the reproach of widowhood for the captivity in Babylon, Ellicott adding that it was out of that bondage that the Lord chose Israel to be his bride. Keil and Delitzsch explain why the encouragement is given now: redemption was before the door, so that Israel was not to fear any more, nor to be overcome by the feeling of shame that belonged to her state of punishment, nor to behave in a way that left no room for hope—a state of things was beginning in which she would have no cause to be ashamed at all, and which would be so glorious that the older shame would simply be forgotten. John Gill turns the command inward, that she is not to fear the fulfilment of what has been promised, however unlikely and unpromising it may seem, since God is able to perform it and no way should be given to a distrustful heart; John Wesley notes that what she was ashamed of was the barrenness and widowhood that had been the matter of her grief, and that she shall not be upbraided with it again.

The reason given is a marriage. Keil and Delitzsch observe first that the widowhood was never real but only apparent, since the husband of Jerusalem was living still; then they take up the plural forms, thy Makers and thy Husbands, and explain them from the plural noun for God, which elsewhere carries plural attributes and plural predicates. By such expressions, they say, which represent all the plurality of the divine nature as inherent in the One, the religion of revelation exhibits itself as embodying whatever is true in polytheism. Gill notices the same plural and reads it of Father, Son and Spirit, though he holds the relation of husband more peculiar to Christ, and unfolds it in stages—betrothed in eternity, openly espoused one by one in conversion, and married publicly in a body at the last day—with the duties belonging to it, that he loves them with a love of complacency and delight, sympathises with them in all their troubles, and nourishes and cherishes them as his own flesh. Ellicott attends to the titles instead: the combination of the two names is characteristic of the earlier part of the book, and the word Redeemer here carries the sense of the next of kin who takes on himself the kinsman’s duty of protection. Wesley draws the practical force out of each title in turn—the Lord of hosts has the sovereign command of all men and creatures, and can therefore subdue the Gentiles to her and make her increase in so prodigious a measure even in her old age; and the last title marks the change, that he is called the God of the whole earth, whereas formerly he was called only the God of Israel.
6:
The figure of a recalled wife is filled out from elsewhere in the prophets. Charles Ellicott finds its starting-point in Hosea and Gomer: the husband has punished the faithless wife by what seemed a divorce, but his heart yearns after her and he takes her back. Keil and Delitzsch notice that the verb commonly used in these prophecies for the call of grace is here used of a call into a relation which existed before but had apparently been dissolved; John Wesley says he recalls her as affectionately as a man his wife of youth. John Gill allows both readings, of a woman who has lost her husband by death and mourns as one forsaken, or of one forsaken by a living husband and holding his bill of divorce, and applies it to the church at its first constitution, when Christ was taken from them by death almost as soon as they were embodied together, and grievous persecutions followed. Ellicott adds that some critics turn the last clause into a question—can she be rejected?—the implied answer being that it is impossible, though he thinks the received rendering adequate.

Matthew Henry begins from the experience rather than the figure. Those espoused to God may seem to be refused and forsaken, and be grieved in spirit under the apprehension of it; those who shall never be left in despair may yet for a time be perplexed and in distress. When God continues them long in trouble he seems to forsake them, which is how their enemies construe it and how they themselves misinterpret it; and God owns that he has done it, for he keeps an account of the afflictions of his people; though he never turned his face against them as against the wicked, he remembers how often he turned his back upon them. He is careful with the word little: not that God’s wrath is ever a little thing, for who knows the power of his anger, but little in comparison with what they had deserved and with what others suffer, since he did not stir up all his wrath—and yet his people, sensible of the least degree of his displeasure, are grieved by it. The afflictions are light and for a moment, a cloud that presently blows over; and as he is slow to anger so he is swift to show mercy, the gathering taking its rise from his mercy and not from any merit of theirs. He counts three gatherings—out of their dispersions, into his arms to bear them up, and at last to himself, as wheat into the barn.

The vocabulary is less comforting than the version suggests. Keil and Delitzsch explain that the word rendered wrath denotes an outburst, like the violence of a storm or a clap of thunder; they also correct the grammar of the second verse, where the term is not an adverb meaning momentarily but an accusative of duration. Gill reports the same from the other side: one version renders the phrase great wrath, one scholar takes it for overflowing wrath and another for the heat of wrath—which, he observes, would agree well enough with the bloody persecutions the church endured. Adam Clarke adds the textual detail: some versions render in a little anger; the word for moment is omitted by several witnesses and seems to embarrass the sentence rather than help it. He notes too that three manuscripts read thy commiserator where the received text has thy Redeemer. Ellicott sets the historical and wider senses side by side: the words point to the seventy years of exile as a transient interruption of the everlasting mercies, and spiritually they have manifold fulfilments in the history of individuals, of the Church, and of mankind. Keil and Delitzsch say the same of the small moment: it carries us to the captivity, small beside the duration of the love that received the church back again.
9:
The oath is the whole point of the comparison, and the commentators divide over what exactly is being compared. John Gill reports that some copies join the first two words into one, so that the sense becomes as the days of Noah, a reading the Targum, the Vulgate and the Syriac follow; he thinks both readings may be kept and joined, giving as the waters that were in the days of Noah. The meaning either way, he says, is that the dispensation towards his people at the time the prophecy refers to is like the dispensation towards Noah and his family, the love he bears them like the love he bore him, and the covenant made with them like the covenant made with him. Adam Clarke works the same variant harder. The two words were formerly written as one, and taken apart they signify for as the waters, taken together as the days; a manuscript and some editions have the single form, several ancient versions acknowledge that their copies vary here, and in one of his own manuscripts the letters appear to have been intended as one word until a much later hand pointed them as two. Of the two he prefers the waters, and observes that the ancient versions support it. Charles Ellicott finds the verse interesting for two other reasons: it shows the writer’s knowledge of the book of Genesis, and it is one of the few references to the Deluge outside that book in the Old Testament. He concedes that Genesis speaks strictly of a covenant rather than an oath, but thinks it idle to make a difficulty of words which, used of a divine act, are almost interchangeable; and he takes the words to have found their fulfilment not in any earthly city but in the heavenly Jerusalem. John Wesley keeps to the plain force: the covenant of grace and peace made with her shall be as certain and perpetual as the one made with Noah, that there should never be another flood to drown the world, and the wrath sworn against is wrath so far as to forsake her utterly.

The second verse presses the same security further by naming what would have to fail first. Gill takes the departing mountains literally of earthquakes and of the last day, when the earth shall be dissolved and the firmest and most durable things in it with it; comparatively, so that these shall sooner depart than the kindness and covenant of God; and figuratively of revolutions in kingdoms and states, adding that a commentator interprets mountains and hills of the kings of the nations. Keil and Delitzsch render the verbs as concessive—the mountains may depart, the hills may shake—and say that the grace and the covenant of peace stand as firm as the mountains of God, without departing from Jerusalem and without shaking, and that they will be fulfilled; not by force or by enchantment, but by a church that must pass through sufferings until it has attained the form answering to the glory promised it on oath, the old Jerusalem coming forth as a new one out of the furnace of affliction. Ellicott prefers the same concessive rendering, notes that the bold hyperbole recurs in the Psalms, in Jeremiah and in the Gospel, and traces the phrase covenant of peace to Numbers and forward into Ezekiel, remarking that peace here includes well-nigh all that is wrapped up in the salvation of the New Testament. Wesley ends where Gill begins, that the mountains shall sooner depart from their places than any kindness depart from her, that God will not cast off his Christian church as he cast off the church of the Jews, since the new covenant is established upon better and surer promises than the old, and that he does this not for her own merits but merely for his own grace and mercy.
11:
The address begins from the condition, not the promise. Matthew Henry reads it as the church reduced by providence: an afflicted and indigent society, tossed like a ship driven from her anchors into the ocean where she is ready to be swallowed by the waves, comforted by no friend and by no prospect of deliverance. That was the condition of the Jews in Babylon and afterwards under Antiochus, and is often the condition of Christian churches—without are fightings, within are fears. Yet God notices her when she is most disconsolate, for in all their afflictions he is afflicted. John Gill reads the same words of the first Christian churches, chiefly poor, afflicted by false teachers who made schisms, stormed by violent persecutors, and uncomforted in the sense that no prince of the earth protected them, so that what comfort they had was internal and spiritual; though he thinks the words fit still better the church under papal persecution. Keil and Delitzsch say the same for the city: the church whose metropolis is Jerusalem is sunk in misery, driven with tempest like chaff of the threshing-floor, scorned rather than comforted by man. But that will be altered, and Jerusalem will rise from the dust like a glorious building of God.

The building materials are then described, and the commentators divide over how literally to press them. Keil and Delitzsch render the first term as stibium and quote a remark they call apt, that the stones are laid in the likeness of an elegant woman who paints her eyes. Charles Ellicott identifies the same word as the black powder of antimony or manganese used by women in the East on eyelids and eyebrows to enhance the brilliancy of the eyes, and takes it here as the setting of the sapphires. He calls the verse the first germ of the idealising symbolism of the new Jerusalem, notes its echo in the book of Tobit, and says it takes its highest form, excluding all thought of a literal fulfilment, in the Revelation. He corrects windows to pinnacles, and thinks it probable, as with the twelve gems of the breastplate, that each stone had a symbolical significance beyond its beauty—sapphire representing the azure of the firmament, the rubies and carbuncles answering to the fiery glow of the divine love and the divine wrath. Adam Clarke resists exactly that. The stones seem to him general images of beauty, magnificence, purity, strength and solidity, agreeable to the ideas of the eastern nations, never intended to be scrutinised as if each had some precise spiritual meaning; he cites the same passage of Tobit as a parallel in manner, not as a key.

Gill reads the stones for what they do. He canvasses the mineralogy first—that some sorts of the stone named were valued for their clearness like glass, that the stone which now bears the name is not lucid enough to make windows of, that several versions render it jasper, and that some take crystal to be meant. Figuratively these design the ministers of the gospel, who are the lights of the world, and the ordinances by which spiritual knowledge, joy and comfort are let into the souls of men. John Wesley declines the mineralogy altogether, remarking that the proper signification of the Hebrew names of precious stones is unknown to the Jews themselves and that it may suffice us to know this was some very clear and precious stone. Henry draws the moral the others leave implicit: never was this literally true, but it intimates that the glory of the New Testament church shall far exceed that of the Jewish, not in external pomp but in the gifts and graces of the Spirit; and that what the children of this world lay up among their treasures the children of God make pavements of and put under their feet, as the fittest place for it.
13:
The promise of a taught people is read by everyone as the heart of the chapter, and the commentators differ mainly over the means. John Gill begins from who the children are—those born in the church and nursed up at her side, the children of God by adoption, which is made manifest by regeneration—and insists on the word all, from the least to the greatest. They shall be taught of the Lord himself, he says, by his ministers, word and ordinances as the means, and by his Spirit as the efficient cause; and he itemises the curriculum, that they are taught to know themselves, their vileness and sinfulness, their folly and weakness, their want of right counsels and the insufficiency of their own, and then to know Christ and the way of salvation by him, so knowing him as to believe in him, receive him and walk on in him. He dates a first accomplishment in the first times of the gospel and a further one in the latter day, when there will be a greater effusion of the Spirit and the doctrines of the gospel will be taught and understood more clearly and fully. Charles Ellicott sharpens the rendering rather than the doctrine: more accurately, shall be the disciples of Jehovah—words our Lord quoted as fulfilled in his own disciples. John Wesley keeps both halves in view: taught not only outwardly by his word but inwardly by his Spirit; and the peace promised is inward peace arising from the clear discoveries of God’s love and reconciliation to us, wrought by the spirit of adoption, which is given more abundantly under the gospel than under the law, and outward peace, safety and happiness besides.

The establishment that follows is taken two ways, and the difference matters. Gill offers both. It may mean established in the righteousness of Christ, from which the peace just spoken of flows, and which is the stability of the church and the security of its members from condemnation—the doctrine of justification by that righteousness being, in the Latin tag he quotes, the article by which the church stands or falls. Or it may mean established in exercising righteousness, doing justice and judgment, which supports a church as it supports a kingdom, since if purity of manners and holiness are neglected a church soon comes to decay and ruin; and such, he adds, will be the holiness of the professors of religion in the latter day that every pot and vessel shall be holiness to the Lord. Keil and Delitzsch combine the two rather than choose. In perfect keeping with grace through righteousness, they say, Jerusalem will then stand firm and impregnable; both its thought and its action will be righteousness, and it will thereby acquire strength. By that reciprocal influence between its moral character and the glory imparted to it, it can and is to keep far away from all thought of oppression and terror, for through divine grace and a corresponding divine nature it has nothing to fear. Wesley takes the plainer civic sense, that her affairs shall be managed with righteousness, which is the glory of any society, and that the oppression removed is oppression either by her own governors or by foreign powers. Ellicott adds a historical edge: on the assumption of the prophet’s authorship, the words stand out in contrast with his own experience of the oppression of Ahaz and of the fear and terror caused by Sargon and Sennacherib.
15:
The closing verses concede that attacks will come, and deny they are commissioned. John Gill takes the denial strictly: not by the Lord, by his command to execute his pleasure, as had sometimes been the case with Sennacherib and Nebuchadnezzar, but so it shall not be when the enemies of Christ and his people gather against them in the latter day. He identifies the agents of that gathering with the unclean spirits of the Revelation who draw the kings of the earth to battle, and applies the whole to the ecclesiastical party he holds responsible; Jewish commentators, he notes, interpret the gatherers of Gog and Magog. John Wesley puts the same point plainly: some will combine and make an attempt against her, but without any such commission as Sennacherib and Nebuchadnezzar had. Charles Ellicott reads it as another contrast with the prophet’s own experience, since the power of Sargon and Sennacherib rested on their being instruments in God’s hands, whereas against the new Jerusalem no such command is given. Adam Clarke disputes the second clause rather than the first. Where the received text has that the gatherer shall fall for her sake, he renders shall come over to thy side, supporting it from Jeremiah and noting that twenty-eight manuscripts, eight of them ancient, have the verb in its more common form.

The reason given for the security is a claim about who made the weapons. Keil and Delitzsch state it as the ground of the whole: Jerusalem will be invincible because Jehovah is its protector. If he has created the armourer who forges a weapon according to his trade—whether an arrow, a sword or a spear, and not, as one commentator supposes, for his own use—then he has also created the destroyer to destroy; the same creative might stands behind both. Gill works the figure out at the forge. The description of blowing the coals is added, he explains, to show that a blacksmith is meant, distinguishing him from the carpenter and the mason, of whom the same word is used and whose crafts require no fire. The comfort for a people surrounded by enemies in arms is that God made the smith who made those arms, not only as a man but as an artificer, giving him all his skill; and he can therefore take that skill away, hinder him from making any, or render useless those already made. Gill reports two other readings of the smith, one taking him for the devil, that great incendiary of mankind, another for a council of war. Ellicott says the verse asserts the same thought: the axe, the hammer and the sword of the great ravagers of the earth are formed by the great Work-Master, who would fashion no such weapon against the new Jerusalem. Wesley extends it from the tool to the hand: both the smith who makes warlike instruments and the soldier who uses them are creatures of God, wholly at his command, and cannot hurt her without his leave.

The last verse widens the protection and names its ground. Gill takes the weapons as all weapons of war, made with a design to destroy the people of God and rendered useless, so that not one prospers to the ruin of the saints. Ellicott finds the implied thought in the second clause, that war comes as the punishment of guilt and is preceded by the cry of accusation; many such cries had risen against the old Jerusalem, and none should be heard against the new. He reads the closing words formally, the solemn asseveration indicating the close of a distinct section. Wesley draws out both deliverances—not only from the fury of war but from the strife of tongues—and reads the final clause as the portion allotted them by God, the righteousness named being the reward of their righteousness, which he gives and will continue.
